mainEntity.name: What should I look for in a Node.js developer for real-time applications?

mainEntity.name: What Node.js frameworks should I look for when hiring a developer?

acceptedAnswer.text: Framework priorities: Express.js (know thoroughly — it's the foundation of the Node.js ecosystem), NestJS (essential for enterprise-scale projects — know the DI system, decorators, modules, guards, interceptors), Fastify (high-performance alternative to Express when raw throughput matters). Also: Prisma (modern ORM — prefer over raw Sequelize), TypeORM (commonly used with NestJS but has quirks), Bull/BullMQ (job queues — essential for background tasks), Passport.js (authentication strategies), Socket.io (real-time). Red flags: developers who only know Express at a basic level without TypeScript, or who haven't used NestJS for any larger project.

mainEntity.name: Can a Node.js developer integrate REST APIs from external services?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes — Node.js's vast npm ecosystem includes official SDKs for almost every external service: Stripe, Twilio, SendGrid, AWS SDK, Google APIs, Slack, HubSpot, Salesforce, and more. For services without SDKs: the axios or node-fetch libraries handle HTTP calls cleanly. Production-quality API integration requires: proper error handling (retry logic with exponential backoff), timeout configuration (don't let slow external APIs hang your server), rate limit handling (respect third-party rate limits, implement your own queue if needed), webhook handler implementation (with signature verification), and integration health monitoring. Ask candidates to explain their approach to handling a flaky external API.

mainEntity.name: What databases work best with Node.js?

acceptedAnswer.text: Database recommendations by use case: PostgreSQL + Prisma ORM: the modern default for relational data (type-safe queries, migration management, visual browser). MongoDB + Mongoose: when your data is genuinely document-shaped (nested, variable structure) and you don't need joins. Redis: caching, session storage, rate limiting counters, Bull Queue broker, Pub/Sub for WebSockets. Elasticsearch: full-text search, log aggregation. The Prisma + PostgreSQL combination is the current gold standard for new Node.js projects in 2026 — type-safe, well-documented, and with excellent migration tooling. Avoid raw SQL strings in Node.js — use an ORM or query builder for security and maintainability.

mainEntity.name: What is the difference between Express.js and NestJS?

acceptedAnswer.text: Express.js: minimal, unopinionated Node.js framework. Gives you routing + middleware, nothing else. You make all other architectural decisions: directory structure, dependency injection, error handling patterns, validation approach. Advantages: simple, fast to start, maximum flexibility. Disadvantages: large projects become inconsistent without enforced conventions; onboarding new engineers is harder. NestJS: opinionated, enterprise-grade framework built on Express. Provides: dependency injection, decorators, module system, guards (for auth), interceptors, pipes (for validation), Swagger auto-generation. Advantages: enforced structure, excellent for large teams, built-in solutions for common patterns. Choose Express for small projects/teams; choose NestJS for larger teams or complex domains.

mainEntity.name: What is Bull Queue and why is it important in Node.js projects?

acceptedAnswer.text: Bull (now BullMQ) is a Node.js job queue library backed by Redis. It handles: background task processing (send emails, generate reports, process uploads without blocking API responses), scheduled jobs (cron-like job execution), delayed jobs (send email 24hrs after signup), priority queues (urgent tasks before normal tasks), failed job retry with exponential backoff, and dead-letter queues for persistently failed jobs. Without a job queue: heavy operations block API response time, scheduled tasks require hacky cron setups, and failed jobs are silently lost. Bull is essential in almost every production Node.js application. A Node.js developer who hasn't used Bull or a similar queue system has limited production experience.

mainEntity.name: What Node.js testing tools should developers use?

acceptedAnswer.text: Essential Node.js testing stack: Jest (test runner — unit + integration, TypeScript support via ts-jest), Supertest (HTTP API testing against running Express/NestJS instances), nock (mock external HTTP calls in tests), factory-bot (generate test data), Playwright (E2E browser testing for full stack verification). A Node.js project without Jest tests is not production-ready. TypeScript compilation errors + ESLint + test suite should all be verified in CI (GitHub Actions) before any deployment proceeds.

mainEntity.name: How do Node.js developers handle authentication?

acceptedAnswer.text: Modern Node.js authentication: (1) JWT (JSON Web Tokens) with short expiry (15min–1hr) + refresh token rotation (refresh tokens stored in httpOnly cookies or a database with revocation capability). (2) Passport.js strategies for OAuth (Google, GitHub, Microsoft) + local (username/password). (3) Bcrypt for password hashing (cost factor 12+). (4) RBAC middleware (check user role/permissions in every protected route handler). (5) Rate limiting on auth endpoints (prevent brute force: 5 attempts per 15 minutes per IP). (6) Session management with express-session + Redis store for session-based apps. Every auth implementation should: validate JWTs on every request, never store passwords in plain text, and log all authentication events (login, logout, failed attempts).

mainEntity.name: Can Node.js handle GraphQL APIs?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes — Apollo Server and Yoga Server are the leading Node.js GraphQL frameworks. Apollo Server integrates with Express and NestJS seamlessly. GraphQL advantages: type-safe schema (SDL definition), clients request only the fields they need (reduces over-fetching), single endpoint vs. multiple REST endpoints, and automatic schema documentation. GraphQL disadvantages: more complex to implement and cache than REST, N+1 query problems require DataLoader, and HTTP caching is harder. When to use GraphQL: complex data graphs where different clients (web, mobile, partner) need different data shapes. When to use REST: simpler use cases, better HTTP caching needs, or teams unfamiliar with GraphQL complexity.

mainEntity.name: How do you handle Node.js application performance issues?

acceptedAnswer.text: Node.js performance toolkit: (1) Event loop lag monitoring (use clinic.js or --inspect to identify blocking operations). (2) Database query profiling (EXPLAIN ANALYZE for PostgreSQL, Mongoose explain() for MongoDB). (3) N+1 query elimination (Prisma include, Mongoose populate, DataLoader for GraphQL). (4) Redis caching for frequently-read, slowly-changing data (product catalog, user profiles). (5) Response compression (compression middleware). (6) Horizontal scaling behind a load balancer (PM2 cluster mode or Kubernetes HPA). (7) Connection pool tuning (pg-pool max connections). (8) Async I/O audit — ensure all I/O operations are properly awaited and no synchronous operations are blocking the event loop.
